Private messaging · Back from the rebuild

White Noise returns. The group stays together.

New native apps for iOS and Android put offline catch-up and reliable group conversations at the centre of the release. The first audience is Nostr.

A preview through TestFlight and Zapstore

White Noise is back with rebuilt mobile apps and a practical promise: return after time offline and find the conversation waiting. The release announcement says devices with the same authenticated history now settle on the same group state, even when changes arrive in a different order.

The project puts it plainly: In plain English: the group stays together, and people get the messages waiting for them when they return.

Both apps and their shared core have been rebuilt. The project says the work accounts for several months without a release, and that friends and family have spent the past several weeks testing real group chats. It expects the new foundation to make subsequent releases more frequent.

Replies, reactions, mentions, encrypted media, multiple accounts and group invitations are part of the package. On Android, the additions include voice dictation, Read Aloud and QR cards for profiles and invites.

On iOS, the announcement describes Face ID protection and screenshot blocking. It says Apple receives a generic notification wake, while the phone constructs the visible message locally; sender, group and message details stay off Apple’s notification service.

White Noise uses the Marmot messaging protocol and end-to-end encrypted groups. An account is a keypair the user controls, with no phone number or email address required. The project describes relays as replaceable, including with one a user runs themselves.

Availability is specific: iOS through TestFlight, Android through Zapstore. The team calls this a sneak peek for Nostr and asks testers to send problems through support inside the app.

Max’s accompanying release note conveys the effort behind the quieter product language: This was so damn hard. The next test is the ordinary one: people leaving a group chat, coming back, and being able to keep talking.

Amber 6.6.5

A separate key for the backup

Amber changes how it encrypts application backups published to relays. The new release uses a dedicated key derived from the account key, instead of encrypting the backup directly under the user’s main identity key.

The release notes describe why that matters: an app with a remembered permission to decrypt NIP-44 messages could fetch the old backup event and read its contents, including app connection secrets and local keys. The dedicated backup key closes that route for newly published backups.

There is a transition: existing identity-encrypted backups still restore through a fallback until the next backup publication overwrites them. Installing the release and replacing the old backup are distinct parts of that change.

The update also restores a missing prompt: after logging out and back in with backup publishing disabled, Amber should once again offer to restore.

Dispatches

Zapstore · A prototype

Bring the search home

Zapstore’s version-two experiment starts with an analogy: a Bitcoin node syncs blocks and queries locally; an offline map downloads its tiles. An app store could likewise pull release bundles and answer searches on the device.

The project reports an early prototype written afresh in Kotlin, with faster browsing and search. The privacy claim is more concrete: For update checks, no need to reveal your installed app set to any remote server.

Tor by default is also in the proposal. This is a promising prototype in Zapstore’s own account, with more details to follow; the post does not announce a public version-two release.

Mostro · Two releases

Choose the node. Reach the solver.

Mostro announces Mostrix 0.3.4 with a picker for trusted instances, clearer order-book filters and payment-method choices that follow the selected currency.

The release also repairs the anti-abuse bond QR flow after Escape or a restart, and lets users manage Blossom media servers much as they manage relays.

A separate announcement introduces Mostro CLI 0.16.2. Its dispute chat can now reach the dispute solver directly. The project also reports a lighter peer-chat envelope, corrected fiat-amount labels and a move to the GPLv3 licence.

An experiment at home

Two months without the subscription

Matt Lorentz reports nearly two months since cancelling Cursor: development work now runs on open-weight models, while a separate personal assistant runs entirely on self-hosted models.

In a follow-up, Lorentz lists the assistant’s actual chores. Hermes and Qwen on an old gaming PC produce morning news and weather, afternoon plant-care reminders, travel research and notices when watched websites change.

The list also includes software security reviews, which Lorentz treats with caution. The useful detail is the routine: an old computer helping with flower-bed drainage, purchases and movie tickets.
